Supply chain professionals will recognize the underlying issue: When suppliers become investors and distribution partners, commercial relationships become harder to evaluate using conventional measures of competitive independence.

Anthropic CEO @DarioAmodei 关于我们首次公开募股的讲话：
我和我的联合创始人创办 Anthropic，是因为我们相信，我们这个时代最强大的技术应当为全人类的利益而构建。
Daniela 和我因一种疾病失去了父亲，而仅仅几年后，这种病就变得可以治愈了。我以生物学开启了我的职业生涯，希望能帮助未来的疗法更早到来。在实验室里，我看到了科学家们在试图理解疾病和开发新疗法时所面对的庞大而错综复杂的难题。
许多能够穿透这片荆棘的科学工具——基因编辑、基因合成、用光控制脑细胞的工具——最初都只是纯粹的想法。换句话说，它们来自思考。来自智能。
人类智能已经让鼠疫、天花和小儿麻痹症在世界上大部分地区成为历史。但对其他疾病的进展对许多患者及其家人来说实在太慢了。从一个伟大的想法到一种疗法可能需要几十年：从最初发现 DNA 中一种奇怪重复模式，到首个使用 CRISPR 治疗疾病的疗法获批，花了很多年。
自然界充满了这样的模式。但我们破译其中大多数的智能太少；科学家太少，时间也太少。现在我们可以构建这种智能。无论是蛋白质折叠、药物设计、癌症遗传学，还是临床试验管理，生物学和医学许多领域的科学家都发现，Claude 能帮助他们在短短几年前所需时间的一小部分内完成研究。我相信足够强大的 AI 与人类协同工作，可以将一个世纪的科学和医学进步压缩到十年。
我不想操之过急。在现阶段，我们只有早期成果。实验和临床试验仍需时间。尽管它们涉及缓慢而笨重的过程，我相信这些过程可以被 AI 大幅加速。我们希望未来有更少的家庭仅仅因为几年之差而错过治愈的机会。
医学只是一个特别生动的例子，但还有许多其他例子。我们的客户——世界上最有雄心的公司、非营利组织和个人——已经在应用我们构建的智能来刺激经济增长；帮助人们摆脱贫困；保护民主和自由社会；甚至让 DMV 这样的日常服务运转得更好。我们很自豪能与他们并肩工作。我对我们未来能共同做的事情极其乐观。
与此同时，我们一直坦诚，这项技术存在非常真实的风险。这些风险包括个人或民族国家对技术的滥用、经济颠覆，以及失去对 AI 系统的控制。我们讨论这些风险，不是因为我们认为它们不可避免，而是因为我们认为它们可以避免。
避免它们取决于构建 AI 的人所做的选择。如果我们对安全漠不关心，与如果我们痴迷于安全，AI 的发展将会有天壤之别。而对安全和公共利益的执着，从一开始就编织进了 Anthropic 的 DNA。从针对生物和网络风险的防护措施，到对齐训练和测试，再到像 X 光一样透视我们的模型内部，Anthropic 开创了理解和引导 AI 系统行为的方法。
还有很多工作要做，最困难的安全工作还在前面。公司令人难以置信的人才使我们能够构建最有能力的 AI 系统，这些人才需要被引导——甚至比以往更加如此——去反复、再三检查这些 AI 系统是安全可靠的。
并且明确地说，我们将控制 AI 系统的训练和部署节奏，需要多长时间就花多长时间，以确保它们安全并始终处于人类控制之下。我们不会屈服于商业或政治压力。今天让公司处于更强大的财务地位，而这只会增强我们做正确之事的决心。
如果我们能证明，在安全方面做出正确选择的同时仍能建立一家极其成功的公司，我们行业中的其他人将受到鼓舞，效仿我们。我们称之为向顶端的竞赛。当向顶端的竞赛正常运作时，哪家公司拥有最好的模型并不重要——每个人都是赢家，因为每个人都在安全地构建。当由领跑者驱动时，向顶端的竞赛效果最好，我们完全希望并期待这样做，但目标是让整个行业变得更好，无论 Anthropic 在任何特定时刻是赢是输。
机器智能的出现是人类历史上最重要的时刻之一，我们有一个难得的机会来塑造它，使其变得更好。
这个时刻比任何一家公司、任何一个国家都更重大。需要我们所有人共同努力，确保这项技术造福于我们以及未来许多代人。从今天开始，我们希望你能加入我们的使命。
Dario Amodei 在 IPO 声明中给出公司使命与安全承诺，包括不受商业或政治压力放缓部署，可了解其立场。

items.excerpt:
Geopolitical tensions, persistent inflation, cautious consumers, and the pervasive impact of artificial intelligence are setting up the new year to be every bit as unpredictable and challenging as 2026.
Operating in the uber-competitive market for logistics services, primarily for transportation, warehousing, and distribution of goods, has never been for the faint of heart. As 2026 concludes and shippers and service providers look ahead to the new year, the most common refrain about what to expect can be summed up in two words: disruption and uncertainty—and how do you plan and adjust for that?
In his company’s annual review of the third-party logistics (3PL) market, Evan Armstrong, chief executive officer of research and advisory firm Armstrong & Associates , said he sees service providers as “cautiously optimistic, and more about margin than volume.” He noted that U.S. 3PL gross revenue in 2025 grew 5.0% to $323.4 billion, with 2026 forecast to hit $351.0 billion. “Much of that 2026 gain is in price,” he said, “meaning [revenue] from record diesel prices [and the associated surcharges] and firmer truckload rates, not [significantly increased] volume.” For 2027, Armstrong is forecasting U.S. 3PL gross revenues of $374.6 billion, an increase of 6.7%.
And as 3PLs settle on strategies and plans for 2027, Armstrong finds them leaning into “increased automation, [higher] productivity, and selective growth, not big headcount or network expansion.”
The Iran War and the wider disruption to global trade lanes has rippled through every node of supply chains, he says. “Longer transit times and higher costs. Freight going around the Cape of Good Hope, adding 10 to 14 days of transit time. Another 8% to 10% of global container capacity tied up in or near the Persian Gulf,” he notes. The biggest hit: the price of diesel fuel, which hit an all-time average high in the U.S. of $6.53 a gallon in late September.
For North American shippers and 3PLs, that has meant surging input and transport costs, more safety stock, rising demand for warehouse space to store buffer inventory, and more volatility in drayage services and port operations as well as tighter truck capacity across both the less-than-truckload (LTL) and truckload sectors.
“Fuel surcharges are lifting gross revenue, while smaller carriers are leaving the market,” Armstrong has observed. Indeed, some 226 trucking operators, generally small carriers with 20 or fewer trucks, filed for bankruptcy last year.

items.description: Data-center growth exposes weaknesses in freight-only planning. Learn how equipment lead times, site readiness and commissioning dependencies reshape. The post The Data Center Boom Is Exposing the Limits of Conventional Logistics Planning appeared first on Logistics Viewpoints .
items.excerpt:
The build-out of AI infrastructure is often discussed in megawatts, capital expenditure and computational performance. But those metrics become commercially meaningful only when a completed, connected and commissioned facility can serve demand. A missing transformer, delayed cooling component or unavailable rigging crew can hold an entire project off the revenue line. This is why data-center logistics cannot be managed as a collection of freight shipments; it must be engineered into the construction and commissioning schedule.
A new facility may require power transformers, switchgear, cooling systems, backup generators, modular assemblies, servers, and extensive cabling. Some items are large and difficult to transport; others are scarce, customized, or constrained by manufacturing capacity. A delivery delay can be amplified when the equipment sits on a critical installation path. The resulting cost is not merely an extra day of trucking. It may be idle construction crews, deferred commissioning, or a missed commercial deployment. The conventional purchasing approach of buying freight independently from project schedules is poorly suited to this environment. Transport and engineering decisions must be coordinated well before equipment is ready to ship.
In its 2026 global data-center outlook , JLL reported that more than half of projects in 2025 encountered construction delays of at least three months. Grid connections, equipment lead times, skilled trades and the ability to coordinate physical execution all matter. A logistics plan should therefore identify the components and permissions that determine when equipment can be energized and tested, rather than optimize every shipment against an identical on-time-delivery target.
A practical control model begins with a component-level critical path. For each transformer, switchgear assembly, cooling module and server rack, the team needs a verified manufacturing milestone, inspection requirement, transportation plan, site-access window, installation dependency and commissioning handoff. items.excerpt:
Runway 介绍了逐步把软件交付各环节交给智能体完成的实践。智能体 10 月驱动了 38% 的合并 PR（6 月仅 0.1%），首次批准等待中位数从超过 2 小时降至约 5 分钟；AI 单独批准的 PR 回滚率约千分之一，低于人工批准的约 1/200。
Runway 逐站交代了让智能体接管软件交付各环节的做法与验收标准，读者可对照借鉴这套可迁移的工程方法。
AI 让写代码变快了，但代码审查却成了工程师们的瓶颈。下面是我们如何一步步把交付流水线交给智能体，以及数据说明了什么。
每个月，智能体编写的代码占比都在上升，拉取请求审查的队列也随之变长。审查机器人能发现问题，但每发现一个问题，改动就要退回再走一轮审查，最终拉取请求还是得等人来批准。
今年夏天，在我们核心 API 仓库中，花在智能体编写代码上的人工审查占比增长了两倍多，达到约五分之一，等待人工批准的拉取请求数量也翻了一番。
Anthropic 工程师 Felix Rieseberg 的“ How to be more ambitious ”启发了我们向前看。我们没有要求智能体写出更好的改动，而是测试它们能否接管软件交付的每个阶段，并且在看结果之前就先定好每个交接环节的评判标准。OpenAI 也描述过 在一个从空仓库起步的产品上发生的类似转变。
10 月我们合并的拉取请求中，有 38% 由云端智能体驱动，而 6 月这一比例仅为 0.1%。9 月到 11 月中旬，首次批准的中位等待时间从两个多小时降到约五分钟，每周合并的拉取请求数量也翻了一倍多。由智能体批准的改动，被回滚的频率并不比人工批准的更高。
从接到任务到上线，中间有七道工序。审查是指阅读改动并提出修改要求；批准则是放行合并的签字。智能体已经在帮忙做第一道工序；下面每一步都会把下一道工序交给它们。
年初的时候，工程师挑一个任务，提示智能体把它写出来并开一个拉取请求，然后等 CI 跑完，再把问题交回给智能体。接着他们得找一位同事来审查。改动一旦合并，主干可能会挂掉，谁先发现谁就得找出原因，要么向前修复，要么回滚。QA 也是手工做的。这些步骤之间的每一次交接都是人的工作，所以智能体写的改动越多，转给工程师的活就越多。
问题所在： 让智能体来写改动，也许能省下我们一个小时的敲代码时间，但随之而来的是整整一个下午的收尾工作：修不稳定的测试、处理 lint 报错、解决合并冲突、回应评审意见。
我们做了什么： 一个内部服务，在云端运行编码智能体，并一路跟进每个拉取请求，直到它全部通过。你给它一个任务、批准它的计划，之后智能体就会写出改动、发起拉取请求、重跑 CI、修复测试、回复评审意见并完成变基。
我们如何确认它有效： 到第三个月，这个服务已经处理了我们 38% 的拉取请求，而且我们的智能体也几乎不需要人工介入。在 11 月上半月合并的 100 个智能体拉取请求样本中，有 78 个没有任何人工提交。
每月合并的智能体驱动拉取请求数：6 月 2 个，7 月 164 个，8 月 268 个，9 月 592 个，10 月 3,130 个，11 月截至目前 1,912 个，全月预计约 3,200 个。
智能体产出可供评审的拉取请求的速度，超过了人们阅读它们的速度，于是评审成了下一个需要交接的环节。
问题所在： 我们的第三方评审机器人缺乏上下文，工程师们于是学会了快速略过它，仍然自己阅读每一处改动。
我们做了什么： 一个 AI 评审器，它拥有与编写代码的智能体相同的上下文，包括计划、diff 以及周围的代码。通常作者也是另一个智能体，因此改动会在编码智能体和 AI 评审器之间来回往返，直到干净为止。
我们如何确认它有效： 在我们的核心 API 仓库中，11 月上半月 AI 评审器发起的评论线程有 93% 被解决或促成了代码改动，高于 9 月的 84%。9 月下旬的一次重建把每次评审的成本降到了约三分之一，同时每周评审量还在上升。
每周评审的拉取请求数从 8 月 10 日当周的 234 个上升到 11 月 9 日当周的 3,177 个。
每次评审成本指数在 9 月 21 日之前保持在 60 到 110 之间，从 9 月 28 日起降至 25 到 37 之间。
问题所在： 让 AI 评审器直接批准能清空队列，但这意味着代码会在没人读过的情况下合并。迈出这一步之前，我们需要证明 AI 的批准与工程师的判断一致。
我们做了什么： 基于风险的批准机制。由一个独立的智能体给每个拉取请求评定低、中、高风险，拿不准时就往高里评，评级决定谁能批准它。起初，我们让 AI 自行批准低风险改动，以及在仓库允许的情况下批准中风险改动。高风险改动交给人工，数据库迁移、密钥和身份认证等代码库的关键区域仍须由代码所有者签字确认。
我们一开始让评审器与人工并行批准，并统计人工提出异议的频率。十月中旬，我们允许仅凭 AI 批准就合并拉取请求。九月到十月间，它批准的 977 个拉取请求中只有 15 个被人提出异议，约占 1.5%，这一日期前后的比例基本持平。
我们如何确认它有效： 首次批准的中位等待时间从九月的两个多小时降到十一月中旬的约五分钟；在我们核心 API 仓库中，AI 评审的合并约有七成仅凭它的批准就完成了。十月到十一月间所有仅凭 AI 批准合并的拉取请求中，只有千分之一被回滚，而人工批准的约为两百分之一。考虑到 AI 批准的大多是较不容易被回滚的低风险改动，我们按风险等级做了对比，发现 AI 批准的表现与人工相当。

items.description: Bolt, Stellantis and Métropole du Grand Paris have announced plans to introduce autonomous mobility services in Greater Paris from 2028, with an initial pilot covering up to five municipalities and potential expansion to more than 30 municipalities by 2030. The project, called the Greater Paris Autonomous Driving Living Lab, has been submitted to the European […]
items.excerpt:
Bolt , Stellantis and Métropole du Grand Paris have announced plans to introduce autonomous mobility services in Greater Paris from 2028, with an initial pilot covering up to five municipalities and potential expansion to more than 30 municipalities by 2030.
The project, called the Greater Paris Autonomous Driving Living Lab, has been submitted to the European Commission’s Autonomous Drive Ambition Cities (ADACities) initiative.
It aims to evaluate how driverless vehicles could complement existing public transport, particularly for first- and last-mile journeys, access to employment centers and travel outside peak hours.
Under the proposed arrangement, Métropole du Grand Paris will coordinate with local authorities, Bolt will manage service integration and operations planning, and Stellantis will provide vehicles based on its Level 4-ready platforms.
Pony.ai has been identified as a potential autonomous driving technology provider, with Nvidia’s Hyperion computing platform and Halos safety system expected to support the solution.
The initial trials would take place in up to five municipalities in north-west Greater Paris, subject to regulatory approval.
The project will assess operational safety, passenger acceptance, integration with public transport and the economic and environmental implications of autonomous mobility.
Markus Villig, founder and CEO of Bolt, said: “Autonomous vehicles will only matter if they solve real transport problems.
“In Greater Paris, we’re working with local authorities and our partners to build a shared service around local needs – from connecting people with public transport to serving journeys that are harder to make today.
“Bolt brings the customer platform and operating experience; our partners bring the vehicle and driving technology. This is another concrete step towards a commercial autonomous mobility service built for Europe.”
Greater Paris has approximately 7.2 million residents, making it one of Europe’s largest metropolitan transport markets.
The partners hope to use the results of the initial trials to determine whether autonomous services could expand across the region.
The longer-term ambition is to move toward commercial operations by 2030, subject to regulatory approvals and the findings of the pilot program.

items.excerpt:
Wayve , Stellantis and Nvidia have announced a collaboration with the French government to accelerate the development and introduction of autonomous vehicles in France, with plans to support wider adoption across the European Union.
Announced at the Assises du Véhicule Autonome forum in Paris, the initiative brings together Wayve’s AI Driver technology, Stellantis’ Level 4-ready vehicle platforms and Nvidia’s autonomous driving computing architecture.
The collaboration aims to establish France as a European center for autonomous vehicle development, combining artificial intelligence, vehicle manufacturing and computing infrastructure.
London-based Wayve specializes in embodied AI for autonomous driving, while Stellantis will contribute its vehicle engineering and manufacturing capabilities.
The Wayve AI Driver will integrate Nvidia’s Halos operating system on the Hyperion computing and sensor platform, providing a foundation for developing autonomous driving systems.
The initiative also involves cooperation with French authorities, trade unions, city administrations and transport operators to address regulatory requirements, safety and the practical introduction of autonomous mobility services.
Philippe Tabarot, France’s minister of transport, said: “France is committed to adapting its regulatory framework to accelerate the development of autonomous vehicles while maintaining strict safety and data sovereignty requirements.”
Kaity Fischer, vice president of autonomous mobility and operations at Wayve, said: “France is leading the way in preparing for autonomous vehicles, and we’re proud to enter this collaboration at such an important moment.
“By working directly with the French Government and our partners, we can help shape how this technology is deployed safely and responsibly and accelerate its development across the country and entire EU.”
The companies say the initiative will also involve local French partners responsible for transport operations, with particular attention to the implications for workers, passengers and communities.
France is already an important engineering and technology development center for Stellantis, while Wayve sees the country as a potential base for expanding its autonomous driving technology across Europe.
The collaboration forms part of wider efforts to move autonomous vehicle technology beyond trials and toward commercial operations, although no specific launch date or service locations were announced.

Nearly half of operations leaders, 47%, say they’re using AI to improve existing ways of working or to experiment without changing how the work is done. And 72% see more potential for AI to grow revenue than to cut costs.

items.excerpt:
The contest among foundation-model providers and enterprise software suppliers is shifting from model performance to the authority to coordinate operational decisions.
The next consequential decision in supply chain technology may not be which transportation management system, warehouse platform, or planning application an enterprise buys. It may be who controls the intelligence layer that interprets the information in those systems, identifies the problems that matter, and coordinates a response. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, xAI, and other model developers are pursuing that opportunity. Established enterprise software suppliers have no intention of surrendering it.
The distinction matters because a capable language model does not automatically produce a sound supply chain decision. Resolving a freight exception or supplier failure requires reliable records, specialized calculations, contractual constraints, and authority to execute transactions. The strategic question is whether the next generation of intelligence will be directed by foundation-model companies, incumbent software vendors, or an enterprise architecture that combines the strengths of both while retaining control of the operating model.
The Real Competition Is Over Decisions, Not Benchmarks
Recent releases—including OpenAI’s GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2, Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon, and xAI’s Grok 4.7—illustrate the pace of development. The models vary in reasoning capability, speed, cost, multimodal processing, and tool use. Those differences can be commercially important, but a public benchmark tells an executive surprisingly little about whether a system can resolve a delayed shipment or safely authorize a supplier change. Performance has to be evaluated against operational work, not model demonstrations.
A model might interpret a carrier’s email, reconcile conflicting shipment updates, or explain the consequences of a forecast change. It does not thereby become the authoritative inventory record, a transportation optimizer, or an approved purchasing system. Those functions remain embedded in ERP, WMS, TMS, planning, and specialized execution platforms. What AI can add is a system of decisions above those applications: a coordinated layer that assembles evidence, invokes the appropriate tools, evaluates alternatives, and moves an authorized action toward completion.

items.description: Retail inventory optimization is a network design decision. See why the right stock location, fulfillment economics and order promises matter more than. The post Retail’s Inventory Problem Is Not Too Much Stock. It Is Stock in the Wrong Places. appeared first on Logistics Viewpoints .
items.excerpt:
The most expensive retail inventory is not necessarily the inventory sitting on a shelf. It may be stock that is technically available to the enterprise but unavailable to the customer who wants it, where and when the customer wants it. That distinction changes what executives should measure: not simply days of supply or store-level turns, but availability, fulfillment cost, service reliability and margin after the order is completed.
Consider a retailer with 200 stores selling a jacket in eight sizes and six colors. That is 48 combinations before we account for seasonal assortment, regional preferences, or replenishment cycles. Some sizes sell out in Miami while the same items sit in a stockroom in Denver. Customers see a shortage. The company may have more than enough units across its network.
This is one of retail’s persistent operating problems: inventory availability is local, but inventory investment is enterprise-wide. Showrooms and inventory-light stores create an opportunity to change that equation. A location can display representative merchandise, help a customer select a product, and draw sellable inventory from a regional pool. The promise is compelling. Less duplicated stock, broader availability, and fewer markdowns. But before anyone declares the end of store inventory, we need to examine the economics.
Retailers have understood the logic of pooled inventory for decades. When individual locations protect themselves against uncertain demand, each carries safety stock. A shared pool can often support the same combined demand with less total buffer, provided the demand across locations is not perfectly correlated. The improvement is not automatic. It depends on the variability and correlation of demand, lead times, service targets, and replenishment flexibility. A regional facility serving 30 stores might reduce duplicated safety stock for slow-moving items while worsening service if its orders take too long to reach customers.
In the jacket example, maintaining every size-color combination at every location creates an expensive long tail. A showroom could carry fit samples and perhaps the highest-velocity sellable sizes, while less common combinations are held regionally. Our Codex-powered system automates finding and fixing performance issues.
By Okay Zed and Cyrus Forbes, Members of Technical Staff
The staggering pace of agentic development has made traditional approaches to performance engineering unsustainable. To keep up, we built the Performance Factory, an autonomous system that uses the full capabilities of Codex and our models to find and fix regressions at an unprecedented speed. The Performance Factory, which runs in the cloud and automates investigating and resolving performance problems, enables us to keep pace with the ambition of our roadmap.
In the Performance Factory, our engineers define workflows for recurring jobs and write instructions for the Codex agents that carry them out. In particular, the Regression Workflow opens a task when a performance alert fires. An agent investigates the slowdown, records its findings in the task, and proposes a fix for an engineer to review. After deployment, another agent picks up the same task to check whether performance has returned to baseline. From investigating to authoring the fix to verifying mitigation, this first workflow in the Performance Factory has automated the entire process of fixing regressions. In just over three months, the Regression Workflow tracked more than 1,700 investigations and root caused over 600 cases. That’s 17 automated investigations every day.
Here, we’ll share how our use of Codex evolved into what’s now the Performance Factory, walk through our first running workflow, and share early lessons from building and running agent workflows in production.

items.title: Trucking Congestion Costs Reach $128 Billion
items.description: "The cost of operating a truck jumped significantly while at the same time congestion returned to highways, placing near-record costs on trucking, retailers and consumers,” said Jeremy Carmichael of Ruan Transportation.
items.excerpt:
Traffic congestion on U.S. highways added $128.2 billion in costs to the trucking industry in 2024, according to the latest Cost of Congestion study published by the American Transportation Research Institut e (ATRI).
That is $4.7 billion higher than in 2022, but slightly below the record high of $129.8 billion in 2023, as a prolonged freight recession reduced truck mileage.
“Post-pandemic, the cost of operating a truck jumped significantly while at the same time congestion returned to U.S. highways, placing near-record costs on trucking, retailers and consumers,” said Jeremy Carmichael, Ruan Transportation Management Systems Vice President of Operations.
“These costs can be addressed through targeted infrastructure investment in the nation’s most congested freight corridors, and a commitment at every level of government to upgrade our highways and improve supply chain efficiency.”
The 2024 figure marks the third year in a row in which annual congestion costs were above $120 billion. That trend illustrates a post-pandemic trucking environment where operating costs have increased substantially, and traffic congestion has moved closer to pre-pandemic levels.
Prior to the 2020 pandemic, annual congestion costs peaked at $99.5 billion.
In 2024, traffic congestion resulted in 1.24 billion hours of delay, which is the equivalent of 451,615 truck drivers sitting idle for an entire year. The average congestion cost per truck was found to be $7,973.
ATRI’s analysis also found that 6.66 billion gallons of diesel fuel was wasted in 2024 due to congestion, resulting in additional fuel costs of $25.04 billion.
In addition to the national findings, ATRI’s analysis also documented state and metro area delays and related cost impacts. Three of the top ten states had costs of more than $10 billion, led by Texas ($10.92B), California ($10.47B), and Florida ($10.35B).
Combined, the top ten states accounted for more than half (53%) of trucking’s congestion costs nationwide. Additionally, the metropolitan areas with the highest congestion costs included New York City ($7.49B), Miami ($3.69B), and Chicago ($3.54B).
